definitions.definition: The graded arrangement of the whole path for persons of three scopes, first set out in Atiśa's Lamp for the Path.

The complete body of sūtra teaching arranged as a sequence of meditations — from reliance on the teacher through the small, middling and great scopes to calm abiding and insight — so that every teaching becomes personal instruction.

The Kadam instruction for transforming the mind through relative and ultimate bodhicitta — especially equalizing and exchanging self and other and sending and taking — and turning adversity into the path, transmitted in terse slogans.
Mind training as integrated into the great scope of the lamrim and the Guru Pūjā.
Mind training as taught in the Parting from the Four Attachments commentaries and by Tokmé Zangpo.

literal: sending and taking; giving and taking

definitions.definition: The meditation of taking others' suffering and its causes upon oneself and giving them one's happiness and virtue, alternately and mounted on the breath (Seven Points 2.6).
The practice of taking and giving that completes the exchange of self and other, made the heart of practice in the Guru Pūjā.
Taught in commentaries on the third line of Parting from the Four Attachments and in the Thirty-Seven Practices.

equivalents.note: tonglen is the meditative technique that enacts the exchange of self and other taught by Śāntideva

literal: the path together with its result

definitions.definition: Virūpa's instruction, the chief teaching of the Sakya, in which the path is taught together with its result because the result is present in the cause: the three visions and the three continua, culminating in Mahāmudrā.

The impure vision of beings with afflictions, the experiential vision of yogins in concentration, and the pure vision of the Sugatas' inexhaustible ornamental wheel of body, speech and mind — the framework of the common Lamdre path.
The first of the three continua: the all-base (ālaya), the union of clarity and emptiness, which contains saṃsāra and nirvāṇa and is therefore the 'root continuum'.

equivalents.note: the Lamdre 'all-base' is read by Sakya teachers as the mind's clarity-emptiness, not simply the Yogācāra store-consciousness

definitions.definition: The distinctive Sakya view of the Lamdre: the causal continuum, the union of clarity and emptiness, is the ground of both saṃsāra and nirvāṇa, which are therefore not separate in their nature.
The nature of the all-base causal continuum: clarity (the mind's luminous knowing) and emptiness inseparable.
The conventional (clear and knowing) and ultimate (empty) natures of the mind recognised together in Mahāmudrā.
The final Madhyamaka view as Gorampa and the Sakya hold it: freedom from all four extremes — existence, non-existence, both and neither — including clinging to emptiness as a negation.

Accepted as a description of the ultimate only in the sense of freedom from the elaborations of inherent existence and of dualistic appearance to the meditative mind; not as a negation of conventional existence.

The four-line instruction of Mañjuśrī to Sachen: freedom from attachment to this life, to saṃsāra, to one's own purpose, and from grasping — equivalent to dharma practice, renunciation, bodhicitta and the view.

literal: the three (kinds of) persons; the three scopes

definitions.definition: Persons of lesser, middling and supreme capacity, who seek respectively the happiness of saṃsāra (higher rebirth), their own peace (liberation), and the end of all others' suffering (buddhahood).
The organising principle of the lamrim: teachings 'common to' the small and middling scopes are practised as preliminaries to the great scope, not as ends in themselves.

cross_language.note: Bodhipathapradīpa v2 uses a threefold puruṣa (skyes bu) classification

definitions.definition: The determination to be free from saṃsāra, arisen when, day and night, not even a moment's wish for saṃsāra's splendours arises and one seeks liberation; the first of the three principal aspects.
The absence of attachment to saṃsāra (the three realms), second line of Parting from the Four Attachments.

literal: the three principal aspects of the path

definitions.definition: Renunciation, bodhicitta and the correct view (of emptiness as dependent arising), which together make any practice a cause of liberation and omniscience.

What Madhyamaka reasoning refutes: inherent existence (existence from the object's own side, not posited by conceptual designation), which must be identified precisely before its absence can be ascertained.
For Gorampa the object of negation at the ultimate level is not limited to a qualified 'inherent' existence: all four extremes, including existence as such, are negated.
A negation that, having negated its object, implies no other positive phenomenon in its place; emptiness is such a negation of inherent existence.
A negation that, in negating its object, implies another positive phenomenon; the Gelug denies that emptiness is of this kind.
Existence as ultimately real, able to bear ultimate analysis; for the Prāsaṅgika, synonymous with inherent existence and existence by own character, all equally negated.
Meditation that repeatedly investigates its object with discernment — for faith, impermanence, bodhicitta and emptiness — as opposed to placement; necessary, not an obstacle.
Meditation that holds the mind one-pointedly on its object without analysis, used chiefly to achieve calm abiding and to stabilise conclusions reached by analysis.
The fault in which the mind's hold on the object slackens; gross laxity loses clarity, subtle laxity keeps clarity but loses its intensity and is easily mistaken for good meditation.

cross_language.note: Buddhist technical sense; distinct from the Hindu 'laya' (dissolution) recorded under trm:laya

definitions.definition: The fault in which the mind scatters toward attractive objects out of attachment; one of the two main obstacles to calm abiding.

literal: nine ways of settling the mind (Tib. sems gnas dgu)

definitions.definition: The nine mental states of calm abiding — placing, continuous placing, repeated placing, close placing, taming, pacifying, thoroughly pacifying, one-pointedness, equipoise — achieved by the six powers and four attentions.
The sixth step of the seven-point instruction: the resolve to take upon oneself alone the responsibility of freeing all beings from suffering and establishing them in happiness.
The innate apprehension of persons and phenomena as inherently existent, the root of saṃsāra, cut only by the wisdom realising selflessness.
The demon that the Wheel of Sharp Weapons turns the weapon against.
The attitude of holding oneself dearer than others — the 'one' into which all blame is driven, the door to all misfortune.
Distinguished from self-grasping (a wrong view about how the self exists): self-cherishing is an attitude of concern for self over others, reversed by exchanging self and other.
Hope for gain, pleasure, praise and fame and fear of loss, pain, blame and disrepute; practice mixed with them is not dharma.
The human life free of the eight unfree states and possessing the ten endowments, of great value and hard to find.
Contemplated under the impure vision of the Lamdre preliminaries.

literal: the four thoughts that turn the mind

definitions.definition: The preliminaries of mind training — the precious human life, death and impermanence, karma, and the faults of saṃsāra (Seven Points 1.1, as the commentaries explain).
The topics of the impure vision in the Lamdre preliminaries.
The eight tenets Tsongkhapa held to be unique to Prāsaṅgika, recorded by Gyaltsab Je.

literal: disintegratedness; the state of having ceased

definitions.definition: In Tsongkhapa's Prāsaṅgika, the disintegratedness of a thing is itself a functioning thing (dngos po) able to produce effects — how past karma connects to its result without an ālaya.

literal: the four authorities (valid sources) of the Lamdre

definitions.definition: Scripture, the teacher's instruction, personal experience and the historical account (of the lineage), by which the result of the path is established.
Experiences of the yogin in concentration — the content of the 'experiential vision' of the Lamdre — which the Vajra Verses teach one to recognise without clinging.
The name of Atiśa's tradition: every word of the Buddha (bka') is understood as personal instruction (gdams ngag) for practice, with nothing to be set aside.

literal: spiritual friend; (Gelug) doctor of Buddhist philosophy

definitions.definition: 'Spiritual friend' (dge ba'i bshes gnyen), the title of Kadam teachers (Geshe Potowa, Geshe Chekawa).
The degree conferred after years of debate on the five great texts; the highest grade is Lharampa, examined publicly at the Great Prayer Festival.
The preliminaries of mind training, the four thoughts that turn the mind (Seven Points 1.1).
The six preparatory practices of a lamrim session and the preliminary practices (prostrations, maṇḍala offerings, Vajrasattva, guru yoga) done before retreat — as in Tsongkhapa's retreat at Wölkha.
The mind wishing for complete awakening for the sake of all beings, generated after love and the sight of beings' suffering; aspiring bodhicitta grows only with the engaging vow.
The second principal aspect: renunciation held by bodhicitta becomes the cause of buddhahood; generated by the seven-point cause-and-effect instruction or by equalizing and exchanging self and other.
Absence of attachment to one's own purpose (Parting 3); relative and ultimate bodhicitta under the experiential vision.
The concentration without which the superknowledges do not arise, achieved by abiding in its limbs and placing the mind on any one virtuous object.

The concentration, conjoined with the bliss of mental and physical pliancy, in which the mind stays on its object at will; achieved through the nine mental states by abandoning the five faults with the eight antidotes.

The wisdom, conjoined with pliancy induced by analysis itself, that discriminates the nature of its object — above all the selflessness of persons and phenomena; the only means of cutting the root of saṃsāra.
The yoga of the perfection of wisdom, joined with method, meditating without conceptualization on the absence of own-nature.
The absence of own-nature of the aggregates, elements and sense-bases, known as unborn; realised by Candrakīrti's instruction; not grasped by conceptual valid cognition.
The mere absence of inherent existence, a non-affirming negation, compatible with and established by dependent arising.
Freedom from elaboration of the four extremes (Gorampa); in the Lamdre, emptiness in union with clarity.

In Madhyamaka analysis, inherent existence (rang bzhin gyis grub pa) — existence from the object's own side — is the object of negation; 'svabhāva' in the sense of the final nature of things (emptiness) is accepted.

The 'king of reasons': because things arise in dependence (on causes, parts and conceptual designation) they are empty of inherent existence; seeing it as unfailing while destroying all grasping completes the view.
In the Vajra Verses, dependent arising (rten 'brel) of body and path — outer, inner and ultimate — through which the path is completed.
One only, indivisible; dharmatā established as nothing at all; realised non-conceptually, 'seeing by not seeing' (Satyadvayāvatāra 4–9).
The emptiness of inherent existence, found by a reasoning consciousness analysing the final mode of existence; an object of knowledge.
Beyond the scope of mind and words, free from all elaborations (Gorampa).
Twofold, false and correct; correct conventional truth is what, unexamined, arises, perishes and performs functions; it is the ladder to the ultimate and must not be disparaged.
What is found by conventional valid cognition; existent, though not inherently; Prāsaṅgika does not divide it into correct and false from its own side, only relative to worldly cognition.
The reasoning by which the Prāsaṅgika draws out the unwanted consequences of the opponent's own assertions, since no subject is established as inherently existent for both parties.

An inference whose subject, reason and example are established as appearing alike to both parties by valid cognition relating to inherently existent objects; used by Svātantrikas, rejected by Prāsaṅgikas (third of the eight difficult points).
For Gorampa, Prāsaṅgika and Svātantrika differ only in whether such inferences are used to generate the view in others, not in the view realised.
The result continuum of the Lamdre, reached through the four result-empowerments; for Sakya Paṇḍita, only the wisdom born of empowerment and the two stages is the Mahāmudrā the Buddha taught.
Approached through sūtra (emptiness of mind as taught by Nāgārjuna) and through mantra (the clear light of great bliss).
In the Lamdre, the all-base consciousness as the causal continuum that contains saṃsāra and nirvāṇa; when purified it is great awakening.
Prāsaṅgika does not accept an all-base consciousness distinct from the six consciousnesses (first difficult point); the 'all-base' of the Seven Points is read as the mind's emptiness.
The master's empowerment, required for tantric practice after pleasing the teacher; the secret and wisdom empowerments are not to be taken by celibates.
In the Lamdre, empowerment of cause (ripening), path (the four empowerments meditated in four sessions) and result (the four result-empowerments of omniscience).
The necessary door to the mantra path, received from a qualified master with the vows and pledges.
Buddhists accept perception and inference; but emptiness is not realised by them taken as conceptual cognitions — they were set up to refute opponents (Satyadvayāvatāra 10–13).
Only perception and inference, as Dharmakīrti taught, with universals as conceptual constructs (Treasury of Reasoning).
Conventional valid cognition establishes conventional existence even for Prāsaṅgikas; inferential reasoning is a means of realising emptiness.
The teacher, reliance on whom in thought and deed is the root of the path; qualified by the ten qualities of the Mahāyānasūtrālaṅkāra.
To be relied on while bad friends are abandoned (Jewel Garland 12).
The fitness of body and mind for virtuous use; its arising, mental then physical, marks the achievement of calm abiding, and analysis-induced pliancy marks insight.
The stage of visualising oneself as the deity in the maṇḍala to purify ordinary appearance and conception, ripening the continuum for the completion stage.
Part of the path of the method continuum in the Vajra Verses ('the generation stage and the rest').
The stage working with the winds, channels and drops to manifest the clear light and illusory body; in the Guhyasamāja, the five stages.
In the Lamdre, the practices on the body as method continuum by which the elements gather and the grounds are traversed.

notes: Restricted practices belong here; only definitions are recorded.

definitions.definition: The thirteenth ground of the Lamdre, the final result, at which one is omniscient and awakens with a retinue.
The only correct sense of emptiness: every phenomenon, including the ultimate, is empty of its own inherent existence; the Gelug rejects 'other-emptiness' as a permanent ultimate.

Gorampa holds the self-empty view in the form of freedom from extremes; Shākya Chokden valued it for cutting conceptual elaboration while also affirming the other-empty view for meditative experience.
For Gorampa, Dolpopa's other-emptiness is the 'eternalist' Madhyamaka; Shākya Chokden accepted an other-empty reading of the Maitreya texts as the view for meditative experience.
Rejected by the Gelug as positing a truly existent ultimate.
Dharmatā 'not established as anything', one and indivisible; all the teachings flow toward it (Satyadvayāvatāra).
Recollected at waking and rested in, free of elaboration, before sleep (Caryāsaṃgrahapradīpa).
In the Vajra Verses, when consciousness dissolves into clear light there appears something like a cloudless sky.
The subtlest mind, manifested in the completion stage and at death, which when joined with the realisation of emptiness is the mantra Mahāmudrā.
The spiritual teacher relied upon as the root of the path, seen in guru yoga as inseparable from the Buddha (Tsongkhapa as Lobsang Thubwang Dorje Chang).

The good teacher who confers the bodhisattva vow is skilled in the rite, abides in the vow, and has patience and compassion (Lamp 23–24); the tantric master is to be pleased with service and gifts (Lamp 64).
The absence of an inherently existent self of persons and of phenomena, differing only in the basis; both are realised by śrāvakas too (fifth difficult point).
Meditating on selflessness is meditating on wisdom; selflessness meditated alone, without method, does not bring awakening quickly.
